newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik leader, rebel colonel agree to talk - official.
newsitem.headline: Tajik leader, rebel colonel agree to talk - official.

text.p: Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov will hold peace talks on Wednesday with mutinous colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, a presidential spokesman said.

"In the next few hours, a meeting will take place between Rakhmonov and Khudoyberdyev but the time and place are secret," Zafar Saidov, Rakhmonov's press secretary, told Reuters by telephone in the capital Dushanbe.
"Rakhmonov and Khodoyberdyev spoke by telephone last night. Both sides have said the conflict can only be resolved by peaceful means".
Saidov said it had been quiet overnight in the Fakhrobad valley, 25 km (15 miles) south of Dushanbe, where government forces clashed with Khudoyberdyev's troops on Tuesday.
The renegade colonel had begun to withdraw some armour south to his headquarters near Kurgan Tyube, some 120 km (80 miles) from the capital, Saidov said.
Khudoyberdyev, 34, commander of an elite government armoured brigade, has mutinied twice before in as many years.
He moved his armour towards Dushanbe at the weekend in the wake of fighting between two rival warlords in the capital, one of whom appears to be backing the government, at least for now.
The latest clashes show Rakhmonov's grip on power as tenuous as ever and the impoverished former Soviet republic far from the peace craved by its 5.7 million population.
Gun law has seen Tajikistan divided up into a complicated patchwork of independent fiefdoms under the control of armed groups like those in neighbouring Afghanistan.
The renegade colonel has not revealed his motives but he is counted by Western diplomats as a potential coup maker.
"I'm not trying to move on Dushanbe," Khudoyberdyev told Reuters by telephone on Tuesday. "Government forces provoked us by moving toward Kurgan Tyube -- we had to defend ourselves".
On Sunday, Rakhmonov issued a three-day ultimatum to Khudoyberdyev to lay down his arms or face "destruction".
There have been no reliable casualty figures, although the International Committee of the Red Cross said at the weekend it had provided medicine for 40 wounded in Dushanbe.

The eruption of fighting on Saturday was not linked to the republic's armed Islamic opposition, with whom the government signed a peace accord in June aimed at ending four years of civil war. That conflict claimed tens of thousands of lives.
Khudoyberdyev said aircraft had bombed Kalininabad, a town near his base.
He lost control of a strategically important aluminium smelter west of the capital to the presidential guard on Monday.
Russia, which deploys 20,000 troops in the Central Asian state and which fears unrest along its unstable southern rim, has been cautious in its reaction to the fighting.
On Tuesday, the predominantly Russian peacekeeping force in Tajikistan fielded by the Commonwealth of Independent States said it would stay neutral and take no part in the conflict.
